runs.output:
== three are open before main runs ==
stdin  is fd 0
stdout is fd 1
stderr is fd 2
nobody in this program opened them. They came with the process.

== open spends the lowest free slot ==
open("/dev/null") -> 3
open("/dev/null") -> 4
open("/dev/null") -> 5
the same file three times, three different slots

== close refunds the slot, and the next open takes it ==
close(4)
open("/dev/null") -> 4
4 again, not 6: the slot close gave back is the lowest free one

== a leak: slots nobody refunds ==
opened 10 more without closing any; the last one is fd 15
on rv6 that is all 16 slots. The next open fails, although /dev/null
is right there. Nothing failed where the close was forgotten.
close those 10, then open("/dev/null") -> 6

== the number says nothing about what is behind it ==
read(fd 3, 64 bytes)  -> Ok(0)   /dev/null is always at its end
write(fd 7, 13 bytes) -> Ok(13)   and swallows every write whole
a file, a terminal, a pipe, /dev/null: all of them are read(fd, buf).

== three reads, two lines ==
read -> 6   buf[..6] is "hello\n"
read -> 3   buf[..3] is "ok\n"
read -> 0   buf[..0] is ""
6 and 3 are both short of 512, and neither one is the end. 0 is.

== the bytes past n are left over ==
buf[..3]  is "ok\n"       the second read
buf[3..6] is "lo\n"       the first read's tail: nothing cleared it
buf[..6]  is "ok\nlo\n"   what a reader that ignores n passes on
`lo` was never typed on the second line. Only n says which bytes are real.

== the mistake: treat a short read as the end ==
read -> 6   got "hello\n"
1 read, then it quit. `ok` was typed and never read.

== a buffer smaller than the line ==
read -> 4   small[..4] is "hell"
read -> 2   small[..2] is "o\n"
read -> 3   small[..3] is "ok\n"
read -> 0   small[..0] is ""
the terminal kept `o\n` for the next read. A full buffer is not a line either.

== a file ends with a short read too ==
read -> 512
read -> 512
read -> 76
read -> 0
1100 bytes. The read that got the last 76 said 76, not 0.
Only the read after it, the one that returned 0, said the file was over.

== 1 MiB through three buffers ==
    1-byte buffer  1,048,576 reads, then the 0: 1,048,577 calls
  512-byte buffer      2,048 reads, then the 0: 2,049 calls
 4096-byte buffer        256 reads, then the 0: 257 calls
512 bytes is 0.2% of the calls a 1-byte buffer makes

== the first factor of 512 is nearly all of it ==
     1 -> 512   saves 1,046,528 calls
   512 -> 4096  saves 1,792 calls
  4096 -> 65536 saves 240 calls   (16 left)
512 to 64 KiB removes 2,032 of the last 2,048 calls, at 128 times the memory

== what the buffer costs: one 4 KiB stack page ==
  512 bytes =  12.5% of the stack   fits, with room for everything else
 1024 bytes =  25.0% of the stack   fits, with room for everything else
 4096 bytes = 100.0% of the stack   the whole page: nothing left for any other local
 8192 bytes = 200.0% of the stack   does not fit: sp runs off the page
that is why cat and wc use 512 bytes and grep uses 1,024.

== on rv6: a kernel that returns at most 128 bytes ==
  512-byte buffer      8,192 reads
 4096-byte buffer      8,192 reads
past 128 the count stops falling: the kernel, not the buffer, sets it.
the loop is the same on both. Only the number of trips changes.

== the input: 30 bytes in a file on fd 3 ==
input = "mount /\nstart the shell\nready\n"
the buffer is 16 bytes. read hands back at most 8; write takes at most 5.

== the loop, on the stingy kernel ==
upcase(..) = Ok(30)
read  returned [8, 8, 8, 6, 0]
write returned [5, 3, 5, 3, 5, 3, 5, 1]
fd 1 got "MOUNT /\nSTART THE SHELL\nREADY\n"
8 bytes in, then write took 5 and write_all went back for the 3.

== the same loop, on a generous host ==
upcase(..) = Ok(30)
read  returned [16, 14, 0]
write returned [16, 14]
same output: true. The kernel chose the calls; the loop chose nothing.

== bare write: every call says how many, and nobody listens ==
upcase_bare(..) = Ok(30)
write returned [5, 5, 5, 5]
fd 1 got "MOUNTSTARTE SHEREADY"
20 of 30 bytes arrived, and the function still said Ok.
on the host every write is taken whole, so every test of this passes.

== a write that takes 0 is an error, not a loop ==
upcase(..) = Err(Error(-1))
read  returned [8]
write returned [0]
without the `n == 0` check, write_all would ask again forever.

== gives up at the first failure ==
  fd 2 | cat: gone.txt: No such file or directory
  $? = 1
the status is right, and todo.txt was never printed.

== lets the last file decide ==
  fd 2 | cat: gone.txt: No such file or directory
  fd 1 | buy milk
  $? = 0
both lines are right, and the 0 is a lie: a file was missing.

== remembers any failure ==
  fd 2 | cat: gone.txt: No such file or directory
  fd 1 | buy milk
  $? = 1
the transcript, exactly. The 1 describes the run, not the last file.

== why the complaint goes to fd 2 ==
$ cat gone.txt todo.txt > both
  the screen gets fd 2: ["cat: gone.txt: No such file or directory"]
  the file `both` gets fd 1: ["buy milk"]
the redirect moved fd 1 only, so `both` holds data and nothing else.

== the shell reads the status ==
  grep -q ERROR log -> 0 (some line matched): `&& echo read the log` runs
  grep -q ERROR log -> 1 (nothing matched): `&& echo read the log` is skipped
  grep -q ERROR log -> 2 (a file would not open): `&& echo read the log` is skipped
grep's 1 is the answer `no`, not a failure. A grep that always said 0
would make every `if grep ..` take the same branch.

== one byte ==
  exit(  1) -> $? = 1
  exit(  3) -> $? = 3
  exit(255) -> $? = 255
  exit(256) -> $? = 0
  exit(257) -> $? = 1
the status reaches the shell as one byte. Return the number of failed files
and the 256th failure reads as success. cat says 1 for any failure.

== one char, two bytes ==
'ñ'.len_utf8()         = 2   one char, two bytes
"año".len()            = 4   len counts bytes
"año".chars().count()  = 3   chars decodes them first
size_of::<char>()      = 4   a char is not a byte
size_of::<&str>()      = 16  and a &str is a pointer and a length,
size_of::<&[u8]>()     = 16  exactly like a &[u8]. Only the promise differs.

== the bytes of a file holding año and a newline ==
  61  01100001  ASCII
  C3  11000011  part of a longer char
  B1  10110001  part of a longer char
  6F  01101111  ASCII
  0A  00001010  ASCII
5 bytes for 3 letters and a newline. `wc` reports 5.

== one to four bytes ==
  a  1 byte(s)  01100001
  ñ  2 byte(s)  11000011 10110001
  €  3 byte(s)  11100010 10000010 10101100
  🦀  4 byte(s)  11110000 10011111 10100110 10000000
a first byte of 0xxxxxxx is ASCII; 110, 1110 and 11110 say 2, 3 and 4 bytes.
every byte after the first starts 10.

== a search for b'\n' cannot land inside a character ==
b'\n' at [4, 10]
bytes >= 0x80 at [1, 2, 7, 8]   the two ñ, two bytes each
0x0A has its top bit clear, and no byte of ñ does. They never collide.

== b"-n" is bytes; "-n" is a str ==
b"-n"                  = [45, 110]   a &[u8; 2]
arg == b"-n"           -> true
arg == "-n".as_bytes() -> true   the same two bytes, reached from a str
b'a' = 97, 'a' as u8 = 97, 97u8 as char = 'a'
a u8 and a char never compare directly. RUN  ./show-errors.sh e0308

== matches! tests a byte against several patterns ==
  rv6 boots
  ..d..vv..   v = a vowel, d = a digit
matches!(0xC3, b'a'..=b'z') = false   ñ's bytes are not letters to a byte test

== when you really want characters, you pay for a check ==
from_utf8(&"año".as_bytes()[..2]) = Err(Utf8Error { valid_up_to: 1, error_len: None })
from_utf8_lossy of the same bytes   = "a�"
a read that ends between C3 and B1 hands you exactly that.
wc -m, which counts characters, has to decode every byte to answer.

== one feed of the whole input ==
feed("one\r\ntwo\r\n") -> pairs = 2

== the same bytes in two chunks, state carried ==
after "one\r"        after_cr = true   pairs = 0
after "\ntwo\r\n"    after_cr = false  pairs = 2
2, the same as one feed. One row per chunk, each starting from the row above.

== the same chunks, state forgotten ==
after "one\r"        pairs = 0
after "\ntwo\r\n"    pairs = 1
1. The \n that opens chunk 2 met a fresh `false`, and that pair vanished.

== every place a read could end ==
  split at  0:               "" | "one\r\ntwo\r\n"  carried 2  forgetful 2
  split at  1:              "o" | "ne\r\ntwo\r\n"   carried 2  forgetful 2
  split at  2:             "on" | "e\r\ntwo\r\n"    carried 2  forgetful 2
  split at  3:            "one" | "\r\ntwo\r\n"     carried 2  forgetful 2
  split at  4:          "one\r" | "\ntwo\r\n"       carried 2  forgetful 1   <- wrong
  split at  5:        "one\r\n" | "two\r\n"         carried 2  forgetful 2
  split at  6:       "one\r\nt" | "wo\r\n"          carried 2  forgetful 2
  split at  7:      "one\r\ntw" | "o\r\n"           carried 2  forgetful 2
  split at  8:     "one\r\ntwo" | "\r\n"            carried 2  forgetful 2
  split at  9:   "one\r\ntwo\r" | "\n"              carried 2  forgetful 1   <- wrong
  split at 10: "one\r\ntwo\r\n" | ""                carried 2  forgetful 2
the carried count is 2 at every split. The forgetful one is wrong only where
a read ends between \r and \n, and the kernel, not the program, picks that.

== what the state costs ==
size_of::<bool>() + size_of::<usize>() = 9 bytes, for a line or a terabyte
that is O(1) state: the same variables whatever the input's length.

== the input, and a 16-byte buffer ==
"abc\ndef\nghijklmn\nopqrstuvw\nxyz"   30 bytes, five lines, the last with no \n
the kernel hands it over in reads of 14, then 10, then whatever is left.

== abc and def: one read, two lines ==
refill   read(fd, &mut buf[0..]) -> 14
         [a b c \n d e f \n g h i j k l . .]   len 14
return   "abc"                                 start 4
return   "def"                                 start 8
the second call made no read. Its \n was already in the buffer.

== ghijklmn: the tail moves to the front, the read goes behind it ==
before   [a b c \n d e f \n g h i j k l . .]   start 8, len 14
compact  [g h i j k l . . . . . . . . . .]   start 0, len 6
refill   read(fd, &mut buf[6..]) -> 10
         [g h i j k l m n \n o p q r s t u]   len 16
return   "ghijklmn"                            start 9
`ghijkl` came in one read and `mn` in the next. The caller sees one line.

== the rest, and a last line with no \n ==
before   [g h i j k l m n \n o p q r s t u]   start 9, len 16
compact  [o p q r s t u . . . . . . . . .]   start 0, len 7
refill   read(fd, &mut buf[7..]) -> 6
         [o p q r s t u v w \n x y z . . .]   len 13
return   "opqrstuvw"                           start 10
before   [o p q r s t u v w \n x y z . . .]   start 10, len 13
compact  [x y z . . . . . . . . . . . . .]   start 0, len 3
refill   read(fd, &mut buf[3..]) -> 0
return   "xyz"                                 no \n, and still a line
return   None
the read that returned 0 did not end the lines. The call after the last one did.

== what it cost ==
4 reads for 30 bytes, through 16 bytes of storage.
each line was a slice of that one array. Nothing was copied out, and nothing grew.

== pop until None ==
  top = 30
  top = 20
  top = 10
pop() answered None, so the loop ended. stack = []

== the same loop, spelled out ==
  top = "grep"
  top = "sh"
  top = "init"
one call, one pattern, per turn. The first value that fails it ends the loop.

== any pattern will do, not just Some ==
  first = 'r', 2 byte(s) after it
  first = 'v', 1 byte(s) after it
  first = '6', 0 byte(s) after it
`[first, tail @ ..]` fails on an empty slice, and that ended the loop.

== a line source, driven by hand ==
  "ls"     2 byte(s)
  "cd /"   4 byte(s)
  ""       0 byte(s)
  "exit"   4 byte(s)
5 calls for 4 lines: the last call is the None that ended the loop.
the empty line came back as Some(""). Empty is a line; None is the end.

== leaving early: break ==
  header "Host: rv6"
  header "Accept: */*"
3 calls, and the body was never asked for.
`break` and `return` leave a `while let` like any other loop.

== two ranges ==
(1..5)  = [1, 2, 3, 4]      stops before 5
(1..=5) = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]   up to and including 5

== where a 2-byte needle can start in a 5-byte line ==
  h e a r t
  ^ ^         start 0
    ^ ^       start 1
      ^ ^     start 2
        ^ ^   start 3
0..=(5 - 2) is 4 starts. 0..(5 - 2) is 3, and never tries start 3.

== contiguous: ear is in heart, not in era ==
"heart".contains("ear") = true
"heart".find("ear")     = Some(1)   it starts at 1
"era".contains("ear")   = false   all three letters, not in one run

== the last start is the one people skip ==
"syslog".find("log") = Some(3)
last start = 6 - 3 = 3
(0..3).contains(&3)  = false   so a scan over 0..3 misses `log`
(0..=3).contains(&3) = true
`logfile` matches either way. Only lines that END in the needle go missing.

== two sizes to decide before counting ==
"heart".contains("")   = true    an empty needle is found in every line
"".contains("")        = true    even in an empty one
"he".contains("heart") = false   longer than the line: no start at all
its last start would be 2 - 5, and a usize cannot hold -3:
  5usize.checked_sub(2) = Some(3)
  2usize.checked_sub(5) = None
  2usize.saturating_sub(5) = 0   not a fix: 0..=0 would still try start 0

== what 2 - 5 does on usize, in a debug build ==
  panicked: attempt to subtract with overflow
catch_unwind(|| 2 - 5) = Err: it panicked
a release build wraps to a number near 2^64 instead, and the first index
that uses it panics anyway. On rv6 either one prints the single word panic.

== a 10 GB log, made up on demand ==
size  10,000,000,000 bytes
lines 500,000,000 of 20 bytes each
read so far: 0 bytes, in 0 reads

== the first line: one read ==
read -> 1024
first line: "line 0000000001 ok."
read so far: 1,024 bytes, in 1 read
the same read holds lines 2 through 51 whole, so they would cost no more.
that is 0.0000102% of the file. The other 9,999,998,976 bytes were never made.

== what reading to the end would cost ==
9,765,625 reads of 1,024 bytes, then one more that returns 0
a program that reads everything and prints only the first line gives the
same output as the one above, and pays for all 9,765,625 of them.

== a source that never ends ==
yes: read -> 1024, first line "y"
after 1001 reads, has read ever said 0? false
`yes | head -n 1` finishes only because head stops asking.
a reader that waits for 0 here waits forever.
